nodes.question: What do the return levels estimate in the context of this study?
nodes.answer: The return levels estimate the amount of precipitation extremes that is expected to be equaled or exceeded once in a certain time period (e.g., 10 years, 50 years, or 100 years).
nodes.paragraph: II of Supplementary information). We model the excess part of precipitation extremes from the threshold with GPD and estimate the return level of precipitation extremes. Our aim is to investigate concurrent changes in extreme precipitation patterns under the Arctic warming scenario using the POT method. By analyzing the trend of Arctic temperature, we are able to identify the transitions that may represent regime changes, e.g., from low precipitating to extreme precipitating periods. In our analysis, the year 1994 appears to be a year of transition. Based on this information, we split the whole time period into two periods, (a) before 1994 and (b) from 1994 to 2023. We also analyze and plot return levels to estimate the amount of precipitation extremes during specified return periods. These return levels describe the amount of precipitation that is expected to be equaled or exceeded once in a certain time period (e.g., 10 years, 50 years, or 100 years). A visualization of these return levels provides a probabilistic framework for understanding and measuring the intensity of rare precipitation occurrences, and thereby assisting the assessment of extreme event risks.

nodes.question: What are the two perspectives from which studies differ in their approach to measuring the impact of extreme weather events?
nodes.answer: The two perspectives are data measurement of event occurrence and methodological estimation of the impact on household welfare.
nodes.paragraph: 2020 ; Sam et al. 2021 ). The impact of climate-induced weather events on household welfare at the micro-level has been the subject of an overwhelming number of studies in the literature.3 Even though these studies provide valuable insights into the extent to which households are affected, carrying out proper cross-study comparisons and drawing definitive conclusions regarding the quantitative impact on welfare is challenging owing to their use of different types of data and methodologies. For example, from a data perspective, there are differences in how studies measure the occurrence of an extreme event, whether by simply indicating the event incidence, deriving climate and asset-based damage functions, or using ex-post damage assessments (Kumar et al. 2023 ; Nguyen et al. 2023). From a methodological viewpoint, there is also variation in how studies econometrically estimate the impact on household wel - fare, including their treatment of extreme weather variables, modeling of standard errors, and the inclusion of appropriate control variables (Hsiang 2016 ; Berlemann and Tran 2020 ; Albertini et al. 2022 ). The purpose of this paper is to present a common framework in terms of (i) geo-spatial modeling the damages due to extreme climate events, and (ii) the use of damage proxies and subsequent challenges in terms of obtaining quantitative estimates through econometric tools and data type.

nodes.question: Why is it challenging to identify the economic impact of weather events?

nodes.question: What challenges exist when evaluating data from weather surveillance radars?
nodes.answer: Data quality and coverage differ between years, countries, and radar stations, which requires careful consideration for specific use cases.
nodes.paragraph: Data quality and coverage differs between years, countries, and radar stations, so care must be taken when evaluating data for each specific use case. Despite these challenges the datasets are currently the most comprehensive of their kind in Europe and open new avenues in understanding continental scale movements of aerial animals. Background & Summary Since the second world war, the airspace across the world has been monitored by an ever-growing network of silent sentinels, constantly interrogating the skies. Specialized radars monitor all forms of movement in the air, and one of the most widespread networks globally is that of weather surveillance radars. Their main purpose is to quantify meteorological phenomena such as precipitation and monitor storm systems, but weather radars also measure other things aloft in the lower atmosphere. As our abilities to analyze and store the huge amounts of data gathered by weather radar networks increase, new possible applications arise. One application that has seen a steep rise in use is the extraction of biological targets from weather radar data, information that is immensely useful for a broad variety of fundamental and applied biological and ecolog - ical questions1,2 As weather radars detect all aerial fauna, from insects3 to birds4 and bats5, they can continuously monitor the movements of animals in the air.

nodes.question: Who maintains the server referred to as BALTRAD?
nodes.answer: The server is maintained by the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute (SMHI).
nodes.paragraph: This server is maintained by the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute (SMHI) and further referred to as BALTRAD European PVOL data are generally not publicly available. Access is granted to members of the ENRAM consortium (including authors of this paper) by meteorological institutes of many OPERA member countries (i.e. the 18 countries covered by the data, as well as Austria and the United Kingdom) through a license agree - ment. It states that PVOL data cannot be distributed further and can only be used for the purpose of extracting animal migration information for scientific research These restrictions do not apply to derived VP/VPTS data. For the BALTRAD_VPTS 28 dataset, we obtained PVOL data from BALTRAD. For the UVA_VPTS29 dataset, the University of Amsterdam (UvA) obtained PVOL data as part of several research projects related to avia - tion safety and wind energy, from three national meteorological services: the Royal Meteorological Institute of Belgium (RMI), German Meteorological Service (DWD) and Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (KNMI). nodes.question: What is the primary purpose of the communication regarding storm Gudrun?
nodes.answer: The primary purpose is to provide an overview of key research themes that have emerged in response to the storm and to highlight the critical role of research and monitoring infrastructure in generating valuable insights for forest sciences from this event.
nodes.paragraph: Now, two decades later, it is timely to re ect on the legacyof storm Gudrun to forest science. This short communi- cation aims are twofold: (1) to provide an overview of key research themes that have emerged in response to the stormand (2) to highlight the critical role that research and monitoring infrastructure has played in enabling the gen- eration of valuable insights for forest sciences from thissingle destructive event. Our search consisted of twodistinct but overlapping efforts that consisted of one search that focused on scienti C articles in general, and one search that focused on scienti C articles involving forests.
